thread:
Anna L: Quick Q — writing a small shell script + a PowerShell wrapper to switch CLI profiles non-interactively across CI and dev machines. I keep hitting keyring/askpass popups on Windows. What’s the recommended secure pattern for ephemeral tokens and profile swapping? I tried `redwood login --profile team` + `export REDWOOD_TOKEN=...` but Windows still prompted a GUI.

Michael B: For CI we avoid OS keyrings entirely — write the token to a temp file with restrictive perms and point the CLI at it. Example pattern: create a temp creds file, set `REDWOOD_CONFIG` (or `REDWOOD_PROFILE_FILE`) to that path, run the command, then shred the file. Also add a `--non-interactive` flag to the CLI invocation. We usually do something like:

```sh
TMP=$(mktemp -p /tmp redwood-creds.XXXX)
echo '{"token":"'$TOKEN'","profile":"team"}' > $TMP
chmod 600 $TMP
REDWOOD_CONFIG=$TMP redwood api call ... --non-interactive
rm -f $TMP
```

Sophie T: If you need Windows support, translate to PowerShell and avoid keyring backend. Use short-lived tokens (TTL 15m) and rotate them from your auth service. Example PowerShell snippet:

```powershell
$tmp = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName()
Set-Content -Path $tmp -Value ($tokenJson)
icacls $tmp /inheritance:r /grant:r "$env:USERNAME`:R"
$env:REDWOOD_CONFIG = $tmp
redwood api call --non-interactive
Remove-Item $tmp
```

Ryan C: Also make sure to set an env var to disable interactive helpers: `REDWOOD_CLI_NONINTERACTIVE=1` or pass `--no-ui`. We added that in our CI runners to suppress any accidental prompts. For local dev, a small wrapper that falls back to interactive if no env var found is nice.

devex-bot: devex-bot: Note: internal helper script available — `devex/tools/cred-swapper.sh` does tempfile creation, chmod, and cleanup. See https://git.internal/redwood/devex/cred-swapper (internal).

Anna L: Thanks — good call. One follow-up: any concerns about tokens leaking (process list, logs)? Is file vs env var different risk profile?

Michael B: Avoid CLI args (they show up in ps). Env vars can leak in CI logs if not masked; make sure runners mask secret envs. Files are safer if you set restrictive perms and delete immediately. Also make tokens short-lived and rotate automatically — audit logs catch bad use.

Sophie T: For Windows keyring prompts specifically, we set `REDWOOD_KEYRING_BACKEND=none` in our PowerShell wrapper so the CLI doesn’t attempt to call into WinCred. That plus `REDWOOD_CLI_NONINTERACTIVE=1` solved most askpass popups for us.

Anna L: Perfect, I’ll implement a temp-file + noninteractive wrapper for both bash and PowerShell and try short TTL tokens. I’ll report back if the askpass shows up again. :thumbsup:

Ryan C: If you want, I can paste our company wrapper later — it’s ~30 lines and handles Windows perms + cleanup.

Anna L: Would appreciate that, thanks everyone!
